the deep structure is less usable than the broad structure, especially for users with low working memory.
the use of deep menu structures is more demanding of users’ working memory resources than the alternative of broad, shallow menus.

the design of speech-based interfaces and, in particular, with the design of auditory menus.
the design of auditory menu structures for speech-enabled interactive voice-response (IVR) systems.
the design of auditory menus for speech-based interactive voice response ( IVR) systems.

, when designing an IVR menu, the best strategy is to create a broad structure with fewer menu levels and more menu options at each level.
a broad menu structure is more efficient than a deep structure.
a deep menu structure is more difficult for the average user than a broad menu structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a deeper menu structure is more demanding on working memory resource than a broader menu structure.
the design guideline that advises limiting IVR menu lengths to five or fewer menu items because of constraints on human working memory is not supported by the evidence.
a broad menu is more efficient and more effective for users.
The main takeaway from our work is that
designers should be careful to avoid deep menu structures and should instead focus on broad menu structures that are easier for users to remember.
, in the context of auditory menus, a deeper structure is not necessarily better.
, when possible, designers should use a broad menu structure to minimize working memory load and improve user performance and satisfaction.
